Guidelines contradict one another: the American College of Physicians (2017) includes acupuncture among the nonpharmacological options for low back pain, based on low-quality evidence, whereas the NICE NG59 guideline (2016) recommended not offering acupuncture for low back pain. EAV (Voll electroacupuncture) and bioresonance claim to measure the electrical conductance of the skin at points and to be able to detect allergies, infections or organ imbalances. Controlled studies have not shown that these measurements reliably distinguish people with and without allergies or other conditions; the device gives values that can be influenced by electrode pressure and skin moisture. These devices can lead to false diagnoses or unnecessary expense. Ryodoraku, a Japanese method of measuring conductance, raises similar questions about reliability.

There are two practical ways to measure. The first uses the person's own fingers: the width of the interphalangeal joint of the thumb is about 1 cun; the width of the four fingers held together, measured at the level of the middle joint of the middle finger, is about 3 cun. Marma comes from Ayurveda; marmas are vital points, associated with anatomical structures (joints, vessels, nerves), considered in tradition to be points where "Prana" accumulates. Marma therapy uses gentle pressure, sometimes with oils. Tradition speaks of 107 marmas; similarities with acupuncture appear here, but the theory is different. What they have in common: all work with pressure, have an energetic theory and are, in practice, forms of therapeutic massage. What differs: the conception of the body, the physical style and the training of practitioners. Research on them is limited and of variable quality; there is modest evidence for reduced pain and tension with massage and soft manipulation, but not for the energetic theory. Treat them as comfort care, with the same precautions as in acupressure.

The meridians (jingluo) are, in the TCM tradition, channels through which Qi circulates. The twelve main meridians bear the names of the Zang-Fu organs: Lung (LU), Large Intestine (LI), Stomach (ST), Spleen (SP), Heart (HT), Small Intestine (SI), Bladder (BL), Kidney (KI), Pericardium (PC), Triple Burner (TE), Gallbladder (GB) and Liver (LR). To these are added two important midline vessels: Du Mai (GV, along the line of the back) and Ren Mai (CV, on the front of the trunk). The codes are the WHO ones, which you will always use.
